analysis.one_liner: Makes it harder for employers to label workers independent contractors, so they can unionize.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: introduced with 8 cosponsors, it died in the Senate labor committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the National Labor Relations Act so that workers count as employees with collective-bargaining rights unless the employer can prove three things: the worker is free from company control, the work is outside the company's usual business, and the worker runs a genuinely independent business of the same kind. It would also narrow who counts as a "supervisor," since supervisors are excluded from union protections. It was referred to the Senate labor committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers currently classified as independent contractors — ride-hail and delivery drivers, other gig and freelance workers — would gain the right to organize and bargain collectively, along with workers mislabeled as supervisors who are currently excluded from union protections [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Presumes that anyone performing services is an employee covered by the National Labor Relations Act unless the employer proves the worker is free from company control, performs work outside the company's usual business, and runs an independently established business — closing off the contractor label companies use to keep workers out of bargaining.

Directly targets the misclassification of employees as independent contractors, which is how many gig-economy drivers are currently treated and which strips them of collective-bargaining rights under current law.

Narrows the definition of 'supervisor' — a category excluded from union protections — by requiring that someone exercise independent judgment in the employer's interest for a majority of their work time, and by dropping 'assigning tasks' and 'responsibly directing' workers from the definition, bringing more workers under the law's protections.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that rely on classifying workers as independent contractors — especially ride-hailing and delivery platforms, staffing agencies, and other businesses built on outsourced labor — would face collective-bargaining obligations and higher labor costs. Genuinely independent contractors could also face pressure to be treated as employees [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The test's second condition — work performed 'outside the usual course of the business of the employer' — could sweep in genuinely independent professionals and freelancers who prefer contractor status, putting their flexibility and client arrangements at risk.

Businesses using contractor labor, including small firms as well as large platforms, would face new bargaining obligations and higher labor costs wherever workers failed the control or independent-business tests.

Narrowing the 'supervisor' definition removes 'assigning tasks' and 'responsibly directing' workers from the test, which could create disputes over who must be included in bargaining units and who manages them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real, specific problem: under current law, workers labeled independent contractors are excluded from collective bargaining entirely. The gains for those workers would have been substantial. The costs fall on companies built around the contractor model, and the broad three-part test risked reclassifying some genuinely independent workers who prefer that status — a tradeoff an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate committee that handles labor law for the entire two-year Congress and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on March 5, 2019, joined by eight original cosponsors — seven Democrats and Independent Bernie Sanders, including Sens. Booker, Gillibrand, Smith, Murray, Merkley, Baldwin, and Durbin.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
That was the last action of any kind: the committee held no hearing, took no markup, and held no vote, and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that classify workers as independent contractors — especially ride-hailing and delivery platforms — kept that model intact, because the bill never advanced far enough to threaten it. Workers who would have gained bargaining rights got nothing.

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled eight original cosponsors.

for.name: Eight original cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on at introduction: Sens. Booker, Gillibrand, Smith, Murray, Merkley, Baldwin, and Durbin (D) and Sanders (I).

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the committee took no action after the referral.

against.name: Ride-hailing and delivery platforms (Uber, Lyft, DoorDash)
against.what_they_did: Have fought employee reclassification of drivers in states and Congress because it strikes at their cost structure; no formal position on this bill appears in the congressional record.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors were Democrats plus Independent Bernie Sanders, with no Republican cosponsors; because the bill never got a vote, there are no roll calls showing where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill's three-part test would make their drivers employees with collective-bargaining rights, striking at the contractor classification that keeps driver wages and benefits off their books. This was the bill's central target.

Businesses built on contract labor would face bargaining obligations and higher costs wherever workers failed the control or independent-business tests, reducing their ability to shift employment costs onto workers.
Reclassifying contractors as employees would expand the pool of workers unions could organize, adding potential members and bargaining units in sectors currently off-limits.
